title: Basic Respiratory-Test Concepts and Patient Instructions

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the purpose and basic concepts of common respiratory tests, including peak flow monitoring and spirometry.
- Recognize the equipment, preparation, and patient instructions involved in respiratory testing and the assistant's role in setup and patient preparation.
- Provide clear, plain-language patient instructions for peak flow and spirometry testing.
- Document respiratory test results accurately and escalate unexpected findings to licensed staff without interpreting results.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A peak flow meter is like a speedometer for your breath: it shows how fast you can push air out in one big puff.

### Question 2

Peak flow helps people with asthma keep an eye on their breathing, like checking a gas gauge to see how full the tank is.

### Question 3

Doctors use spirometry to see how well a person's lungs work, which is especially helpful for a lung problem called COPD.

### Question 4

COPD is an umbrella name for a couple of long-term lung problems that make it hard to get air in and out.

### Question 5

Smoking and breathing in smoke are the main reasons people get COPD, which is why quitting is so important.

### Question 6

FEV1 is a fancy short name for how much air you can blow out in the first second of a big breath.

### Question 7

FVC is like measuring the whole tank of air you can push out after the deepest breath you can take.

### Question 8

Peak flow is one quick number, like a snapshot, while spirometry is a fuller report, like a whole video of the breath.

### Question 9

Peak flow numbers are counted in liters per minute, which tells how many liters of air rush out in a minute at that speed.

### Question 10

The nose clip is like pinching your nose shut so every bit of air has to go through the straw instead of sneaking out your nose.

### Question 11

A peak flow meter is small enough to carry in a pocket, so people can check their breathing almost anywhere.

### Question 12

Spirometry belongs to a family of tests called pulmonary function tests, which are all about checking how well the lungs do their job.

### Question 13

An ECG is like a microphone for the heart's electrical signals, showing doctors the rhythm the heart is beating in.

### Question 14

Your personal best is your own top score when you feel good, like your high score in a game that future scores get compared to.

### Question 15

The number only makes sense if the person really gives it their all, like how far a ball flies depends on how hard you throw it.

### Question 16

We ask patients to blow a few times because one try might be a fluke, and a few tries show the real picture.

### Question 17

The assistant is like a helpful coach and note-taker: they help the patient try their best and write down what happened, while the doctor decides what it means.

### Question 18

Only the trained doctor or provider decides what a breathing number means, just like only a referee makes the final call in a game.

### Question 19

Writing down the number is like keeping a scorecard so the doctor can look back and see how the lungs have been doing over time.

### Question 20

It is like timing a runner, giving them a little help, and timing them again to see if the help made a difference.

### Question 21

Each patient gets their own clean straw-like mouthpiece so germs do not travel from one person to the next.

### Question 22

The zones are like a traffic light in the patient's plan: green means go, yellow means caution, and red means stop and get help, and the doctor sets the plan.

### Question 23

The assistant helps the patient blow correctly and writes the number down, then hands the scorecard to the doctor, who decides what to do.

### Question 24

Stand tall, take the biggest breath you can, wrap your lips around the tube, and blow it out like a big, fast puff of wind.

### Question 25

We ask for three tries and keep the very best one, because the best one shows what the lungs can really do.

### Question 26

Take the deepest breath ever, then blow it out hard and keep going until we say stop, like emptying a balloon all the way.

### Question 27

Sit up tall and wear comfy, loose clothes so your belly and chest can stretch all the way when you breathe.

### Question 28

The doctor may ask patients to skip smoking and big meals before the test so the lungs are at their normal best.

### Question 29

Measure at the same time each day, like brushing your teeth, so the numbers are fair to compare.

### Question 30

When someone is nervous, we calmly explain what will happen first, like walking them through a game's rules before they play.

### Question 31

We explain it in easy words and then ask them to show us they understand, like a coach checking that the player knows the play.

### Question 32

When a number looks different, we write down exactly what happened and quickly tell the doctor, who decides what it means.

### Question 33

If someone gets out of breath and cannot continue, we stop right away and get the doctor, because safety always comes first.

### Question 34

If the patient cannot finish the big blow, we write down what happened and tell the doctor, so the doctor knows the test was incomplete.

### Question 35

If the machine will not show a number, we do not pretend; we set it aside and tell the person in charge so it can be fixed.

### Question 36

Like a fresh straw for every drink, each patient gets a brand-new mouthpiece so germs are not shared.

### Question 37

We clean and put away the device exactly the way the instructions and our office rules say, like following a care tag on a shirt.

### Question 38

We write the exact number, the unit, and when it was taken, like writing the score, the team, and the date on a scorecard.

### Question 39

We keep the very best of the three tries, like keeping your highest jump in a jumping contest.

### Question 40

We write down just the facts, like writing the exact number on a scoreboard and leaving the judging to the referee.

### Question 41

If someone asks whether their score is good, we politely say the doctor will check it, because only the doctor knows what the score means.

### Question 42

Only the doctor changes medicine. If a patient asks, we say we will tell the doctor right away so the doctor can decide.

### Question 43

If we make a mistake on the scorecard, we fix it neatly with our initials and the date, not by scribbling it out or pretending it never happened.

### Question 44

Before the test, we double-check who the person is, like confirming the name on a package before signing for it.

### Question 45

If the device's checkup sticker is out of date, we do not use it; we tell the right person so it can be checked.

### Question 46

For a heart tracing, we ask the patient to lie still and relax, like staying very still for a photo so it does not come out blurry.

### Question 47

Write each reading in a little notebook, like keeping a diary of your breathing, and bring the notebook to the doctor.

### Question 48

Wrap your lips snugly around the tube like a straw so no air sneaks out the sides.

### Question 49

If it hurts or they are too tired to blow, we do not push them; we tell the doctor and let the doctor decide.

### Question 50

Chest pain is a big red flag, so we get the doctor right away, like calling for help when a fire alarm goes off.

### Question 51

Only the doctor gets to say whether a number is normal or not, like only a judge says whether a play is fair.

### Question 52

We note how the patient has been feeling, like writing down the weather before a big game, so the doctor has the full story.

### Question 53

We ask about smoking and medicines because they can change how the lungs behave during the test, and the doctor wants to know.

### Question 54

We can say the zones are like the traffic lights in the doctor's plan, but only the doctor decides which light is showing.

### Question 55

Different meters can be like different gadgets with different buttons, so we follow the manual for the one we have.

### Question 56

Sit up nice and tall like a superhero before you take your big breath, so your lungs have room to work.

### Question 57

If the numbers jump all over the place, we write them down just as they are and tell the doctor, who can figure out why.

### Question 58

We write the results into the official chart right away, like posting a score online as soon as the game ends.

### Question 59

The assistant writes the score down; the doctor decides what the score means, like a scorekeeper and a referee.

### Question 60

Blow like you are trying to blow out all the candles on a birthday cake in one big puff.

### Question 61

We double-check the order and who the patient is, like checking the label and the address before mailing a package.

### Question 62

The assistant is not allowed to decide what the number means or what medicine to use; only the doctor does that part.

### Question 63

We keep the very best try, like keeping your longest jump out of three tries.

### Question 64

If the numbers go down after a new medicine, we tell the doctor and let the doctor figure out why.

### Question 65

If the machine shows an error, we stop and follow the rules or ask for help, like calling tech support instead of guessing.

### Question 66

If someone gets dizzy, we stop and help them sit safely, like pausing a game when a player feels faint.

### Question 67

When a person and a machine both have a problem, the person always comes first; we call for help for the person right away.

### Question 68

We tell the right person in charge, following the office's rules about who to tell, like reporting a problem to the coach, not the bleachers.

### Question 69

What is normal for one person is different for another, so we just write the numbers down and let the doctor do the comparing.

### Question 70

If only two tries got done because of coughing, we write down two tries and the reason, like noting a runner did not finish the race and why.

### Question 71

We write down the before number and the after number, and the doctor looks at both to see if the medicine helped.

### Question 72

If the plan does not seem to match their numbers, we tell the patient to talk to the doctor, who is the one who writes the plan.

### Question 73

The assistant can spot something odd and write it down, but only the doctor decides what it means.

### Question 74

The assistant checks who the patient is, teaches the blow, writes the real number down, and hands it to the doctor, who makes the calls.
